#3413. David Fincher's Rejected Star Wars Movie Pitch Would Have Centered On Two Beloved Franchise Characters

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

His interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:

"I said, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were."

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

"Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened."

Notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:

"I said to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'"

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.

#3412. Sorry Jason And Lucia, These 5 GTA 6 Side Characters Steal Every Scene They're In

From Brian to Yago, we loved interacting with these eclectic side characters

Although Jason and Lucia are the stars of Grand Theft Auto 6 and amazing characters in their own right, there are lots of side characters who steal the show whenever they show up. From folks critical to the main story path to weirdos you meet if you take the time to stop and chat with someone on the side of the road, GTA 6 constantly introduces wild, memorable characters almost every hour.

These side characters make the world of GTA 6 feel more fleshed out, lived in, and representative of all different kinds of kooky folk. They’re a big part of what makes the game special, and we’re thankful that Rockstar Games took the time to make us care about people other than Jason and Lucia. In particular, these five characters emerged as some of the Polygon staff’s favorites.

Brian is the single biggest scene-stealer in GTA 6 for one reason: Stephen freakin’ Root! For years, Root has been one of Hollywood’s ultimate “Hey, it's that guy” character actors. Now, fresh off an extremely well-deserved Emmy win for his role in Widow’s Bay, he brings the same kinetic, frenetic energy to Brian in GTA 6.

The eternal brilliance of Root’s acting comes from the humanity he injects into every character — often people who would be impossible to believe in lesser hands. Like many of Root’s best roles, Brian is a little too wacky for the real world, but there is a clear and nuanced sense of humanity underneath all of that eccentricity. That ethos is reflected throughout the entirety of Grand Theft Auto, and Brian is the key to selling it from the start. —Ari Notis

Of all the side characters Rockstar has introduced in GTA 6, Raul Bautista (voiced by Manny Pérez) is my personal favorite. He commands attention — not through loud bravado, but through quiet, seasoned authority. Raul carries himself around with a sun-bleached cool reminiscent of Don Johnson’s Sonny Crockett mixed with the criminal smarts of Robert De Niro’s Nick Wells from The Score. Raul isn’t the sort of guy who needs to announce himself or make a show of what he can do. As a seasoned bank heister who knows Vice City like the back of his hand, Raul operates with understated confidence and stays deliberately out of the spotlight, treating high-stakes scores like a craft rather than a spectacle.

Living on a boat also shows he’s calculated down to his quarters and can pull anchor and disappear on a dime whenever the heat closes in. What makes him especially intriguing is how little we know about his past. Who knows? He could’ve easily crossed paths with Michael Townley and Trevor Philips during their early heisting days — and maybe even learned a thing or two from them. — Ryan Epps

Midway through GTA 6, just as the heists are heating up, Jason becomes an accidental hip-hop mogul. In a series of missions, Jason is called upon to help promote Real Dimez, an up-and-coming rap duo managed by Only Raw Records. The group immediately steals the show the moment they first appear on screen. Played by real Miami rappers Hood Brat and Krissy Celess, Bae-Luxe and Roxy add some welcome levity to the story as they try to get their big break with a ridiculous single about “booty holes.”

Their missions have Jason doing promo photo shoots, breaking into house parties, and shooting music videos as Real Dimez rise to stardom. In a game that’s almost entirely about complex criminal enterprises, it’s a reprieve to get a side-tale about two musical misfits looking for their moment the old-fashioned way. — Giovanni Colantonio

Jason’s Key Lento neighbor Shirley is a good, kind soul, if a slightly eccentric one. She has her own way of viewing the world, and while it’s certainly centered around a brand of logic unique to Shirley, it’s not a bad thing. She cares about people as much as she cares about her obnoxiously yappy little dog Arugula, and she’s genuinely hurt by the unnecessarily rude comments from Peggy (of “steal her scooter” fame).

Shirley is basically your odd-but-sweet neighbor who you might dread catching the attention of on your way home, but would never dream of showing that dread or turning down a chance to talk to, if only briefly. Hurting her feelings? Inconceivable. And it’s to GTA 6's credit that it encourages you to meet Shirley halfway and be kind to her without judging her oddities. — Josh Broadwell

When I pulled up to my first street race in Vice City, I was not expecting to kick off a whole Fast & Furious-like sidequest in the game. Early on, you meet Yago, a talkative and ambitious racer who just has one problem: he can’t drive very well. Yago takes an instant liking to Jason, who guides him through being a better street racer and drug dealer. What ensues is one of the best male friendships in the game — and one that you can entirely miss.

Yago and Jason’s dynamic is equal parts hilarious and endearing, as Yago constantly teeters on annoying but is so gung-ho and into Jason that you can’t help but love him. He also exposes a softer side of Jason that you otherwise only see through his interactions with Lucia. I won’t spoil how Yago’s sidequests ultimately play out, but that event ultimately recontextualizes his entire relationship with Jason and ends up making him one of the game’s more nuanced characters. — Tomas Franzese

#3411. Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

Any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the big screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very important to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

This idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

In "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and company have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows users to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

The idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

#3410. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

"Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

Was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

There's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is currently working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils."

Cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash."

James Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

The "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:

"There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course."

What about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

Quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is currently scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

#3408. 8 Near-Perfect Fantasy Series You Can Watch In A Weekend

Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team. Since then, she has written for the Perennials and Streaming team, covering a wide range of topics from new releases to old movies and TV shows. Memory is currently a Classic TV writer.  Before joining Screen Rant, Memory was a freelance copywriter who specialized in email marketing and social media management. While she enjoyed her job, her true passion was always movies and TV. When she isn’t writing for Screen Rant, Memory can be found reading, baking (which is one of her passions), or watching her favorite K-drama.

The fantasy genre has become synonymous with stories that require an enormous time commitment to get through. TV shows like Game of Thrones, Supernatural, and The Wheel of Time have made lengthy fantasy storytelling popular, but that does not mean that is all the genre has to offer. Among some of the most beloved fantasy series is a treasure trove of genre shows that only take a weekend to watch. Even with their short run times, these shows deliver an entertainment experience akin to longer series.

The best fantasy shows are not always the longest, but those that tell their stories in a way that leaves a good impression on audiences, regardless of their length. There is always a need for a series, fantasy or not, to introduce a convincing world and characters who make its plot better instead of weighing it down. The most memorable genre shows do this, but the shorter productions do so without requiring audiences to commit to an overwhelming episode count.

One could argue that shorter fantasy shows that can be binged in a day or two tend not to fully explore their worlds, but that is not always the case. Fantasy series with a weekend-length episode count understand their time is limited, so they don't linger on filler. All in all, it is a tricky balancing act to tell a story in a few episodes while still doing justice to what it is trying to say. Fortunately, several fantastic fantasy series have figured out just how to do this perfectly.

Dirk Gently’s Holistic Detective Agency is a Netflix show most viewers have never heard of, but it's a woefully underrated series. Best described as The Dresden Files, but with an incredible duo, the series centers around the delusionally optimistic Dirk Gently (Samuel Barnett) and his reluctant partner, Todd Brotzman (Elijah Wood), as they go about investigating supernatural crimes. Dirk Gently has everything an audience can expect from a fanatsy/sci-fi/mystery series: interesting cases, deep lore, as well as an emotional core.

However, what truly elevates the series from great to excellent is two primary protagonists, Dirk and Todd. Like any memorable TV duo, the two characters have a sort of odd-couple relationship. Where Dirk walks around like a happy puppy, Todd is sullen and doesn’t always see the bright side to everything. It is this contrast in their demeanor that makes the show so interesting and makes viewers excited about what the odd pair will do next.

Several people have grown up reading, watching, or listening to the stories of Cinderella, Snow White, Prince Charming, and many other fairy tale characters. With such tales being so familiar and seeing several iterations over the years, it's difficult to do something new with them that would make viewers notice, as opposed to ignoring them because they've seen the same stories time and again. The 10th Kingdom is perfect because it understood that fairy tales are interesting, but they don’t have to follow the same storytelling formula as those that have come before them.

The series centers around a young woman named Virginia (Kimberly Williams-Paisley) and her father, who are transported from modern-day New York into a magical world consisting of nine fairy tale kingdoms. For a television production released in 2000, The 10th Kingdom has an impressively ambitious fantasy setting. It includes everything that audiences love about fairy tales, but also ensures it adds a bit of a modern touch.

Cartoons are usually frowned upon by most audiences who erroneously believe that live-action offers a better viewing experience. Cartoon Network's Over the Garden Wall disproves this theory by being a masterpiece that tells a surprisingly deep story that delves into everything from the meaning of life, and grief, to the pain of growing up. Initially, Over the Garden Wall plays out like a story about two brothers who get lost in the woods, but it is actually way more than that.

The beauty of Over the Garden Wall is how audiences come away with different versions of what the meaning of the series is. Some viewers believe that the Unknown was a hallucination, while others are convinced that the series was a dream or a metaphor for death. The thing about Over the Garden Wall is that it is open to interpretation. All arguments about what the show means have some merit, which is what makes it such a joy to watch.

Starring David Jason and Sean Astin, The Color of Magic is a two-part British fantasy miniseries based on the first two novels in Terry Pratchett's beloved Discworld series. The story introduces viewers to Rincewind (David Jason), an exceptionally incompetent wizard who has very little magical ability and an even greater talent for getting himself into trouble. His life takes an unexpected turn when he encounters Twoflower (Sean Astin), a cheerful tourist from a distant land who has travelled to Discworld to experience its wonders.

Pratchett’s Discworld novels have one of the best fantasy settings, which ultimately means that they are not easy to bring to life. Thankfully, The Color of Magic gives it a valiant effort, resulting in a world that is so perfectly built that it is easy for non-book readers to see why the Discworld series is such a fan favorite. While The Color of Magic is an exceptional fantasy series that shines for many reasons, Rincewind makes it even better.

Most fantasy stories often revolve around powerful wizards, or individuals destined to save the world. Rincewind is practically the opposite. He is a cowardly, largely incompetent wizard whose greatest talent is running away from dangerous situations. This, of course, makes him one of the most interesting characters in fantasy TV.

It's easy to dismiss Loki as another Marvel Cinematic Universe cash grab, but the Disney+ fantasy series is much more than that. Occurring after the events of Avengers: Endgame, Loki sees the titular character stuck in the Time Variance Authority, an organization that fixes timelines, after he steals the Tesseract. The series is complex, with lots of moving parts, including the TVA and several versions of Loki. But beneath the complexity is a story about someone who has been viewed as a villain but is actually a hero.

Everyone loves a long-running fantasy epic, but sometimes, the best fantasy shows come in bite-sized packages, perfect for a weekend marathon.

Tom Hiddleston is, as one might expect, fantastic as Loki. However, he does not carry the show alone. Owen Wilson as Mobius and Sophia Di Martino as Sylvie are absolutely riveting. Loki is the perfect example of a show that proves that there is always nuance to a character. Granted, the series is a sci-fi and fantasy fan’s dream come true, but it is also an incredibly thoughtful look at a character who finally begins to understand what his purpose really is.

Released in 2024, Dead Boy Detectives is based on characters from Neil Gaiman's DC Comics universe. The eight-episode series follows two teenage ghosts, Edwin Payne (George Rexstrew) and Charles Rowland (Jayden Revri), who decide to remain on Earth after death rather than move on to the afterlife. Instead, they establish a detective agency dedicated to investigating supernatural mysteries and helping spirits resolve unfinished business.

Dead Boy Detectives doesn’t exactly tread new waters when it comes to its supernatural/mystery plot. However, it does set itself apart from others in the genre due to its two primary protagonists. Because the series centers on two teenage ghosts who have decided that death shouldn't prevent them from having careers, it is immediately entertaining.

The series’ main duo give it much of its personality. Charles frequently encourages Edwin to embrace experiences beyond his investigations, while Edwin provides the intelligence and discipline necessary to solve their cases, making the duo a match made in heaven.

Arcane has been hailed as not only one of the best animated shows of the past decade of the past decade, but also as the kind of fantasy series that other shows in the genre should aim to emulate. Premiering on Netflix in 2021, Arcane is mainly centered on the contentious relationship between two sisters: Vi (Hailee Steinfeld) and Jinx (Ella Purnell). However, as the show goes on, it becomes a story about the fight between good and evil and whether good endings can justify wrong actions.

The Netflix original series is a masterclass in world-building. Though the show only has two seasons with 18 episodes, it manages to pack so much into its limited time. The beautifully animated series is brilliant at balancing tension with the complexity of how humans relate to each other. Of course, Vi and Jinx’s relationship is at the center of it, but there are other supporting characters who are just as intriguing as the primary protagonists.

One of the most fascinating things about Arcane is that it never drops the ball. Every episode is perfect, every storyline is carefully woven, and every character gets the time they need to develop and be the kind of protagonists that audiences care about, whether they love or hate them.

Another fantasy series that demonstrates that a great duo is the heart of a memorable story, Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell centers around Mr Norrell (Eddie Marsan), a cautious, scholarly magician who believes magic should be controlled and practiced exclusively by those he considers responsible, and Jonathan Strange (Bertie Carvel), a naturally gifted young man whose extraordinary magical abilities quickly attract attention.

Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell Key Details

Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell excellently incorporates magic into an otherwise recognizable historical setting. The series places supernatural events within an alternative version of Regency-era England. Magic is treated almost like an academic discipline, with its own history, theories, and social expectations. This, in turn, makes it a series that is already ahead of its competitors.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3407. Avengers: Secret Wars Setting Confirmed By Marvel, Spoiling Doomsday

It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a new planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

The Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

The first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

This second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars."

Asked to comment further, Feige said, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

None of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a big shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for new characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

We know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter."

Whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a big screen visit to Battleworld.

#3406. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.
